author: Paid Observer
title: Apple DCF Model - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL)
text:
Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL ), the behemoth has succumbed to the law of large numbers. Growth in sales and earnings peaked years ago. That doesn't mean the stock can't still be an attractive investment opportunity. With half of fiscal '18 in the books, I offer an up-to-date intrinsic valuation of AAPL shares.
Using discounted cash flow methodology, I build a free cash flow to equity (FCFE) model. I look at the cash flows calculated as net income less reinvestment needs, adjusted for debt. Reinvestment needs include capital expenditures and investment in working capital.
FCFE can be thought of as cash that could potentially be returned to shareholders. So by estimating these cash flows and discounting them at the cost of equity, we can get a reasonable estimate of value per share. I will build a base year for the model, using the most up to date trailing 12-month data, and include a typical or normalized year of reinvestment needs.
TTM Numbers To get the most up-to-date numbers possible, I calculated trailing 12-month net income for my base year. The income statement is shown below.
Image: Author's spreadsheet
It's worth noting $53.32B in net income would be the 2nd best year on record, still behind the monster 2015, which brought in $53.39B. However, EPS would be at a new record (and will definitely be a new record in FY '18) after factoring in another 4-5% decline in the share count.
Net Capital Expenditures In assessing Apple's ability to sustain itself, we need to broaden the scope of capital expenditures to include money spent on intangible assets such as patents and licenses, as well as acquisitions.
First, I normalize acquisition expenditures and payments for intangible assets by taking the average over the last 5 years to be $1.56B. Using trailing 12-month numbers, I calculated payments for property, plant, & equipment at $13.15B, while depreciation & amortization is $10.32B. The net of these 2 numbers plus the $1.56B yields $4.39B in adjusted net capex for the base year.
Working Capital I usually calculate a non-cash WC by backing out cash and marketable securities from current assets, and commercial paper and the current portion of long-term debt due from current liabilities. However, AAPL has such a substantial cash and marketable securities balance that non-cash working capital is negative and actually declining.
I could revert to the basic definition of working capital, but the year-to-year change is erratic. I take the 5-year average change of $1.74B as the investment in working capital for the base year. The sum of the adjusted net capex ($4.39B) and the normalized investment in working capital ($1.74B) are the reinvestment needs for the base year ($6.13B).
Net Debt Issuance Equity investors should consider the effects of changes in the debt level on their cash flows. How much of the company's reinvestment needs are being financed by equity, and therefore returning cash flows to equity?
The company has steadily increased its debt ratio up to 26% in fiscal 2017. Management has wisely locked in low interest rates, and at a AAA bond rating, the company has access to the cheapest capital in the market. If we conservatively assume no change in the debt ratio, we can simply multiply our figure for reinvestment needs by (1 - debt ratio) to obtain a figure for the reinvestment needs financed by equity.
The Discount Rate I use the CAPM to estimate the company's cost of equity.
Cost of equity = risk-free rate + beta x (equity risk premium) I use the yield on the US 10-year treasury as the risk-free rate, 2.94% as of June 5, 2018. For the equity risk premium, I consult Aswath Damodaran's website , where he has calculated the implied ERP as of June 1, 2018 as 4.78%.
Using Yahoo Finance historical prices for AAPL and the S&P 500, I calculate daily returns going back 2 years to June 2016. After regressing the sets, the calculated beta is 1.03.
Cost of equity = 2.94 + 1.03 x 4.78 = 7.86% A beta around 1 was expected, especially now that AAPL makes up about 4% of the market cap weighted S&P 500. The cost of equity at 7.86% will be used to discount the cash flows.
Image: Apple
Growth In FCFE Growth is the most difficult thing to forecast accurately for a financial modeler. I could get into how well the iPhone X seems to be selling, or consider possible new revenue-generating projects, or we can simply look at some historical data. When looking 5+ years into the future, it's important to remember to value the business as a going concern.
In other words, the company's past history of reinvesting in the business (including acquisitions, capex, and R&D) has successfully brought them to this point. So the iPhone X is not nearly as important to the valuation of the stock as people make it out to be. After all, there will be an iPhone X1 or whatever.
The company has an impressive history of growth. Over the last 10 years, sales have grown at a compounded average growth rate of 25%. Still impressive, the 5-year CAGR in sales is 8%. Net income has only managed 3% CAGR in the same period, but EPS has grown at 8% due to the company's ongoing major share buyback program. I show some figures for growth going all the way back to 2002 below.
Image: Author's spreadsheet
Considering the rate of deceleration in all categories, a 5% growth rate for the next 5 years in FCFE/share still seems conservative. I calculate a terminal value 6 years out using a perpetual growth rate of 2%.
The Model I aggregate my assumptions and show my calculation for FCFE in the base year. Remember, I am multiplying reinvestment needs by (1 - debt ratio) to simplify net debt issuance calculations. I allow cash flows to grow in the "high" growth phase for 5 years, then calculate a terminal value in year 5 based on the value of a perpetuity using the anticipated year 6 cash flow.
Images: Author's spreadsheet
The present value of the sum of future expected cash flows to equity is $989,360,000,000. I add in the balance of cash and marketable securities and divide by the number of shares outstanding to arrive at a figure for equity value per share. I also conducted some sensitivity analyses involving the most important variables.
Images: Author's spreadsheet
The model predicts AAPL shares are worth about $248. The sensitivity analyses indicate little downside, and a value between $210-$308 is highly likely.
Diversification Of Growth The company continues to deliver exceptional products at impressive margins. The underlying theme that makes this possible is simply that Apple has successfully targeted a segment of the market that can and will pay top dollar for its products. This dedicated consumer base puts a floor on the most bearish case growth scenarios.
In the most recent quarter, net sales were up in every reported product segment (though barely for Macs, which were down on a unit basis), and up in every reported geographical segment. Worth highlighting is the growth in services (up 31% yoy) and other (up 38% yoy). These 2 segments, which include digital content and music services, ApplePay, AirPods, Apple TV, Apple Watch, Beats products, HomePod, and others are showing significant growth outside of the traditional profit centers for Apple.
This is great news for shareholders as the company continues to prove its R&D is paying off. The company also continues to show the ability to turn sales into profits, even in new segments. No doubt the company is already massive, so they will have to continue to innovate in new areas to move the overall growth needle. Incidentally, this is something they have proven to be very good at.
Conclusion Using the most up-to-date numbers possible and conservative assumptions about growth, the model predicts AAPL shares are worth about $248. This would take the company to a market cap in excess of $1.25T, or upside of about 28%. The model predicts Apple's operating assets alone are worth $989B. Even with no growth over the next 5 years, and a meager 2% terminal growth rate, AAPL shares are currently fairly valued. For me, any decline from here is a clear buying opportunity.
Generally speaking, if the market avoids catastrophe, we will see AAPL shares surge past the $1 trillion mark this year. Management just raised the dividend by 15.9%. FY '18 will be a new record in EPS. With another $100B authorized in the share repurchase program, we'll see the share count decline by another 4-5%. The psychology should be bullish.
This is what Benjamin Graham was referring to when he talked about margin of safety. Looks like it's time to stop complaining about lower growth rates and start celebrating record profits.
